
# Recoding variables and crosstabs

Week 8 tutorial goals:

  * Recoding categories: changing and combining categories
  * Turning continuous variables into categories with `cut()`
  * Creating and saving cross-tabs
  * Reversing the scale of a variable

## Set-up

### Make sure you have your project datasets and `W8.R` {-}
You also need `ces2025_small.csv`, the CES file we used in Weeks 5 and 6. Put it in the same folder as `W8.R`.

### Load libraries {-}
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
# install.packages("haven") # if you haven't installed the package
library(haven)
library(sjPlot)
```

### Load data {-}
We start with the smaller CES file from Weeks 5 and 6 (`ces2025_small.csv`).
```{r,eval=F}
ces <- read.csv("ces2025_small.csv")
```

```{r,echo=F}
ces <- read.csv("data/ces2025_small.csv")
```

## Recode categories

Sometimes we want to change the categories of a variable. We can give the categories clearer names, or combine several categories into fewer. We use `mutate()` and `if_else()`, the same as in Week 5.

### Give categories clearer names {-}
In Week 6, we saw that `union` is coded 1 = yes and 0 = no. Sometimes values like "yes" and "no" are easier to work with.
```{r}
table(ces$union)
```

If `union` is 1, the new variable is "Yes". Otherwise it is "No".
```{r}
ces <- ces |>
  mutate(union_member = if_else(union == 1, "Yes", "No"))
```

#### Check the new variable {-}
Every 1 should be "Yes" and every 0 should be "No". People with `NA` for `union` still have `NA`.
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces$union,
         var.col = ces$union_member)
```

### Combine categories: create a region variable {-}
`province` has 13 categories, and some have very few respondents. We can combine provinces into four regions: West, Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic.
```{r}
table(ces$province)
```

#### Create the region variable with `if_else()` {-}
Now we need four categories instead of two, so we build the new variable one region at a time. `%in%` (from Week 4) checks whether a value is in a list: `province %in% c("Alberta", "Manitoba")` is `TRUE` for anyone from Alberta or Manitoba.

* The first line creates `region`. People from the West get "West", and everyone else gets `NA` for now.
* Each line after that fills in one more region. If the test is `FALSE`, we keep what `region` already was.
```{r}
ces <- ces |>
  mutate(region = if_else(province %in% c("British Columbia", "Alberta", "Saskatchewan", "Manitoba"), "West", NA),
         region = if_else(province == "Ontario", "Ontario", region),
         region = if_else(province == "Quebec", "Quebec", region),
         region = if_else(province %in% c("New Brunswick", "Nova Scotia", "Prince Edward Island",
                                          "Newfoundland and Labrador"), "Atlantic", region))
```

#### Check the new variable {-}
Every province should be in one region. The three territories (Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut) are not in any region, so they are `NA`. Only 61 people live there.
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces$province,
         var.col = ces$region)
```

#### Crosstab of region and vote choice {-}
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces$vote,
         var.col = ces$region,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

### Clear environment {-}
```{r}
rm(list=ls())
```

## VDem

### Load Data {-}
```{r}
vars <- c("country_name", "country_id", "year", 
          "v2x_libdem","e_gdppc","v2mefemjrn", "v2pepwrgen")

vdem_selected <- read.csv("Project/VDem/vdem2000_2023.csv") |>
  select(all_of(vars)) |>
  filter(year==2010) 
```

* Variables selected:
  * `v2x_libdem`: Liberal democracy index
  * `e_gdppc`: GDP per capita
  * `v2mefemjrn`: % of female journalists
  * `v2pepwrgen`: Power distributed by gender

### Create ordinal categories using function `cut()` {-}
```{r}
?cut # pull up the documentation for `cut()`
```

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/w8_cut.png")
```

#### Consider this variable: v2mefemjrn (% of female journalists) {-}
```{r echo=FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/w8_vdemExample.png")
```

```{r}
head(vdem_selected$v2mefemjrn)
```


```{r}
cut(vdem_selected$v2mefemjrn, # numeric variable
    breaks=4) |> # either number of intervals OR list of cut points
  head()

cut(vdem_selected$v2mefemjrn, # numeric variable
    breaks=c(10,30,50,70)) |> # either number of intervals OR list of cut points
  head()
```

#### Add the new ordinal variables to the data frame {-}
```{r}
vdem_selected <- vdem_selected |>
  mutate(v2mefemjrn_ord4 = cut(v2mefemjrn, 
                              breaks = 4),
         v2pepwrgen_ord4 = cut(v2pepwrgen, 
                                 breaks = 4))
```

#### Crosstabs {-}
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = vdem_selected$v2mefemjrn_ord4,
         var.col = vdem_selected$v2pepwrgen_ord4,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

#### Export table {-}
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = vdem_selected$v2mefemjrn_ord4,
         var.col = vdem_selected$v2pepwrgen_ord4,
         show.col.prc = TRUE,
         file="crosstabs.html")
```


For your final project, open the html file on your laptops and copy the table into your word document

### Skewed variables {-}
```{r}
ggplot(vdem_selected,aes(x=e_gdppc)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

#### Crosstabs will not display well {-}
```{r}
vdem_selected <- vdem_selected |>
  mutate(e_gdppc_ord4 = cut(e_gdppc,
                            breaks = 4),
         v2x_libdem_ord4 = cut(v2x_libdem,
                          breaks = 4))

tab_xtab(var.row = vdem_selected$e_gdppc_ord4,
         var.col = vdem_selected$v2x_libdem_ord4,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```


#### Alternative using quantile cut points {-}
```{r}
quantile(vdem_selected$e_gdppc, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25),na.rm=T)
```

The new variables end in `_quant4`, so they don't replace the `_ord4` variables we just made.
```{r}
vdem_selected <- vdem_selected |>
  mutate(e_gdppc_quant4 = cut(e_gdppc,
                              breaks = quantile(e_gdppc, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25),na.rm=T)),
         v2x_libdem_quant4 = cut(v2x_libdem,
                                 breaks = quantile(v2x_libdem, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25),na.rm=T)))

tab_xtab(var.row = vdem_selected$v2x_libdem_quant4,
         var.col = vdem_selected$e_gdppc_quant4,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

### Clear environment {-}
```{r}
rm(list=ls())
```


## Canadian Election Study 2025

### Load Data {-}
```{r}
vars <- c("cps25_age_in_years", "pes25_turnout2025", "cps25_govt_confusing")

ces_selected <- read_dta("Project/CES2025/2025 Canadian Election Study v1.dta") |>
  select(all_of(vars))
```

* Variables selected:
  * `cps25_age_in_years`: Age in years
  * `pes25_turnout2025`: Did you vote in the 2025 federal election? (1 = Yes, 2 to 8 = different reasons for not voting)
  * `cps25_govt_confusing`: Sometimes, politics and government seem so complicated that a person like me can't really understand what's going on (1 = Strongly disagree, 4 = Strongly agree, 5 = Don't know)

#### Create a turnout variable {-}
```{r}
ces_selected <- ces_selected |>
  mutate(turnout = if_else(pes25_turnout2025 == 1, "Voted", "Did not vote"))

table(ces_selected$turnout)
```

### Age and turnout {-}

#### Crosstab using age as it is {-}
Age has almost 80 different values, so the crosstab has almost 80 columns. It is very hard to read.
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces_selected$turnout,
         var.col = ces_selected$cps25_age_in_years,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

#### Create age groups using `cut()` {-}
```{r}
ces_selected <- ces_selected |>
  mutate(age_groups = cut(cps25_age_in_years,
                          breaks = c(17, 29, 44, 64, 100)))

table(ces_selected$age_groups)
```

#### Crosstab using age groups {-}
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces_selected$turnout,
         var.col = ces_selected$age_groups,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```

### Reverse scale {-}

For `cps25_govt_confusing`, a higher number means the person finds politics *more* confusing. Sometimes it is easier to talk about a variable when a higher number means *more* of something good, like understanding politics. To do this, we reverse the scale.

First, set "Don't know" (5) to `NA`. Then subtract the variable from (highest value + 1). The scale is 1 to 4, so we subtract from 5:

* 1 becomes 5 - 1 = 4
* 4 becomes 5 - 4 = 1

```{r}
ces_selected <- ces_selected |>
  mutate(govt_confusing = if_else(cps25_govt_confusing == 5, NA, cps25_govt_confusing),
         govt_understand = 5 - govt_confusing)
```

#### Check the new variable {-}
Every 1 in the old variable is a 4 in the new variable, and so on.
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces_selected$govt_confusing,
         var.col = ces_selected$govt_understand)
```

#### Crosstab of understanding politics and turnout {-}
```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = ces_selected$turnout,
         var.col = ces_selected$govt_understand,
         show.col.prc = TRUE)
```
